title: Radar wins at Empress Augusta Bay

facts.text: In the dark early hours of 2 November 1943, Rear Adm. A. Stanton Merrill's Task Force 39 met a Japanese cruiser force off Empress Augusta Bay, Bougainville.
Merrill had four light cruisers, Montpelier, Cleveland, Columbia and Denver, and eight destroyers, four of them led by Capt. Arleigh Burke.
Rear Adm. Sentaro Omori came down from Rabaul with two heavy cruisers, two light cruisers and six destroyers to smash the American transports at the new beachhead.
American radar found the enemy at 2:27 a.m., about 20 miles away, while Japanese lookouts were still searching with binoculars.
Radar directed 6 inch gunfire crippled the light cruiser Sendai, and two Japanese destroyers collided while dodging the shells.
The destroyer Hatsukaze collided with the heavy cruiser Myoko and was later sunk by American destroyers at dawn. Sendai also went down.
USS Foote ran into a Japanese torpedo that blew off her stern and killed 19 of her men. Denver took three 8 inch hits that did not explode.
Omori wrongly believed he had sunk several American cruisers and ordered a retreat at 3:37 a.m. His superiors later relieved him of command.
Just before 8 a.m., more than 100 Japanese carrier planes from Rabaul attacked the task force as it guarded the crippled Foote.
Seeing the sky full of planes, one sailor joked: "Pipe to breakfast; how do you want your eggs?"
Ships' gunners claimed 17 planes and Allied fighters claimed more. The only two bomb hits landed on Montpelier's starboard catapult.
No Japanese ship reached the transports, and the Marines' beachhead on Bougainville was saved.

photoNote: Small file (740 px wide); a larger NHHC scan would help the card. A Japanese plane crashes into the sea ahead of USS Columbia during the air attack on Task Force 39, November 1943. U.S. Navy photo 80-G-44059 (NHHC copy on Wikimedia Commons), public domain. Commons dates it 1 to 2 November 1943; a daylight crash beside the cruisers fits the 2 November morning attack, but the caption does not say so.
